scenes.title: Pat Bennett silently mouths a sentence as 62-WPM text streams across the Stanford monitor
scenes.era: 2023, Stanford Neural Prosthetics Translational Laboratory clinical session, Palo Alto

layout.description: Bright clinical neuroengineering room where a 68-year-old participant sits upright in a powered wheelchair facing a large eye-level computer monitor; two compact percutaneous pedestals above her left ear connect via slim ribbon cables to a rack amplifier while decoded English words stream rapidly across the display at 62 words per minute.

positions.who: Participant Pat (68-year-old mannequin in teal cardigan seated in powered wheelchair)
positions.where: center-left facing the eye-level display screen, silently shaping words with her lips

positions.who: Stanford neural engineer (mannequin in collared shirt and lab badge)
positions.where: seated camera-right beside the neural signal workstation
positions.facing: watching the real-time spike raster and text output
facing Pat with an encouraging nod

props.name: 128-channel percutaneous pedestal connectors and ribbon cable
props.period_detail: two small brushed-titanium cranial ports wired to the BrainGate preamplifier
props.physical_behavior: transmit live neural spike trains into the bedside decoder rack

props.name: widescreen speech-output monitor
props.period_detail: 27-inch clinical display showing cue sentence above and live decoded sentence streaming below
props.physical_behavior: words appear rapidly one after another at 62 words per minute

props.name: two 3.2-mm 64-electrode silicon arrays (bench display model)
props.period_detail: tiny square silicon grids with 64 microscopic platinum-tipped pins beside a centimeter ruler
props.physical_behavior: demonstrate the 3.2-millimeter scale of the cortical sensors

actions.verb_sequence: fixes her gaze on the prompt screen -> gently shapes silent syllables with her jaw and lips -> pauses as the full sentence completes on the monitor
monitors the 128-channel raster plot -> leans forward as decoded text hits 62 words per minute

reactions.reaction: lifts her shoulders and tilts her head warmly as her exact words appear on screen
claps both hands together quietly beside the workstation

scenes.wardrobe: Participant Pat: soft teal knit cardigan over white blouse and dark slacks in a clinical wheelchair. Engineers: crisp lab coat and buttoned Oxford shirt.
scenes.lighting: Clean high-key California clinical daylight illuminating the wheelchair, monitor, and signal rack.
scenes.recognition_hook: A paralyzed woman silently mouths words in a wheelchair while full sentences stream onto a screen in real time at 62 words per minute.

key_visual.description: the paralyzed participant in a wheelchair silently mouths words as sentences stream onto the monitor from cortical electrodes

scenes.title: Slow 15-WPM letter-by-letter eye-tracker bottleneck

layout.description: Home study with an infrared eye-tracking alphabet grid mounted before a wheelchair user staring slowly at one letter tile after another.

positions.where: seated in wheelchair staring intently at individual alphabet squares

props.name: alphabet dwell-selection screen
props.period_detail: on-screen QWERTY grid requiring a one-second stare per letter
props.physical_behavior: fills a single word slowly letter by letter at 15 words per minute

props.name: desk timer
props.period_detail: digital desk timer advancing past 20 seconds for one short phrase
props.physical_behavior: ticks upward while the sentence remains half-finished

actions.verb_sequence: holds gaze on one letter tile -> waits for the dwell ring -> shifts gaze to the next letter

reactions.reaction: slumps shoulders slightly at the slow 15-WPM bottleneck

scenes.wardrobe: Teal cardigan on Pat; casual sweater on caregiver.
scenes.recognition_hook: Spelling letter by letter at 15 words per minute turns a five-second remark into an exhausting wait.

scenes.title: 39-phoneme decoding pipeline vs silent area 44

layout.description: Neuroengineering bench displaying dual cortical placement diagrams (active area 6v vs quiet area 44) and a 39-phoneme probability bar chart.

positions.facing: pointing from the 6v spike raster to the phoneme sequence

positions.where: standing beside the cortical map model

props.name: 3D matte-white cortical placement model
props.period_detail: anatomical brain model marking two arrays on ventral premotor 6v and two on area 44
props.physical_behavior: 6v markers show dense spike traces while area 44 stays flat

props.name: phoneme probability display
props.period_detail: live chart converting spike bins into 39 phonetic sounds and stitched words
props.physical_behavior: bars shift cleanly with each syllable

actions.verb_sequence: traces the spike train from ventral premotor 6v into the phoneme probabilities and language model output

reactions.reaction: nods at the stark contrast between vibrant area 6v and quiet Broca's area 44

scenes.wardrobe: White lab coat and surgical scrubs jacket.
scenes.recognition_hook: Two pea-sized arrays on ventral premotor cortex carry all 39 English phonemes while Broca's area 44 stays nearly silent.

scenes.title: Conversational speed restored across a 125,000-word vocabulary

layout.description: Bright clinical lounge where Pat converses fluidly with two researchers via the live 62-WPM screen.

positions.where: seated in wheelchair facing two researchers across a small table
seated across the table reading and responding immediately

props.name: tabletop conversation display
props.period_detail: angled screen showing natural multi-word replies in real time
props.physical_behavior: updates smoothly as Pat speaks silently

props.name: printed 125,000-word dictionary volume
props.period_detail: thick reference dictionary beside the monitor illustrating unconstrained vocabulary

actions.verb_sequence: attempts a spontaneous joke -> sentence flashes across the screen -> researchers respond immediately

reactions.reaction: lean back in delighted laughter at the natural back-and-forth rhythm

scenes.wardrobe: Teal cardigan on Pat; collared shirts on researchers.
scenes.recognition_hook: Crossing 60 words per minute restores real-time human give-and-take.
